newsitem.title: UK: NatWest looks to squeeze investment bank.
newsitem.headline: NatWest looks to squeeze investment bank.

text.p: Squeezing more out of its capital will be the determining factor in how Britain's NatWest Bank reshapes its investment banking strategy, analysts said on Monday.
"They will do more to reduce the amount of capital in the business...anything the management can do to raise the overall returns would be good news for shareholders," one analyst said.
This had been the thrust of recent briefings by NatWest finance director Richard Delbridge to City of London institutions, he added.
British newspaper reports suggest NatWest will pull back from parts of its NatWest Markets investment banking arm and will soon announce the strategy change, and perhaps management.

The reports prompted an initial 18.5 pence rise in NatWest shares to 815 pence on Monday, although by 1200 GMT they had fallen back to 808 pence. The stock bucked a trend for falling bank shares in the London market.
The strategy review could coincide with a report into embarrassing and costly interest rate options losses at NatWest which surfaced in February.
But a NatWest Markets spokeswoman declined to comment on what she described as "speculation".
NatWest is due to release the results of the three-month probe into how a 90 million pound ($147 million) loss in its derivatives division went unnoticed for nearly two years.

The report was originally due at the end of May but is not now expected to surface until the end of June, once it has been studied by banking supervisor the Bank of England and financial markets watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA).
Both have already received copies of the report by City accountants Coopers & Lybrand and law firm Linklaters & Paines, banking sources said.
The scandal has already led to the suspensions of four senior employees and the withdrawal of millions of pounds in staff bonuses.
It has also cast a shadow over the future of NatWest Markets chief executive Martin Owen, who newspapers said could leave as part of the shake-up.
"It has become clear to NatWest Markets that Martin Owen is a short-dated stock, maturing in August," another analyst told Reuters.
But it was not yet clear if the firm would look internally or to the outside for a replacement.
Insiders at NatWest Markets have played down a strategy meeting held two weeks ago, which they say was an annual fixture and not called specifically to address radical changes in approach.
Analysts said it was no surprise the position of NatWest Markets within NatWest was under review.
"There is continuing and increasing dissatisfaction of institutional shareholders with NatWest," the second analyst said.

This was based on the high cost of running the bank's British business -- which had been partly addressed by a retail banking transformation programme -- and by unresolved questions over NatWest Markets.
NatWest Markets made a return of one percent on risk weighted assets totalling 39 billion pounds, the first analyst said, adding it would attempt to shed the "value-destroying parts of the group".
"The easy way is to look again at the large corporate lending books," he said.
The firm has already attempted to shift billions of pounds off its balance sheet by securitising some of its syndicated loans.
But the scheme was not particularly well received by the market and industry sources said NatWest had struggled to sell the debt.
It has also encountered problems syndicating low-margin but large loans, forcing it to take on more of the debt that it would want to, they added.

While NatWest's rival Barclays has been more aggressive in reducing its exposure to large corporate loans, NatWest Markets has continued to take on new business, which eats up capital but is fiercely competitive and earns little margin. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
